title: Showcase: the last word
summary: The formal three-round recorded debate on a motion they pick, five minutes on the season book, three season sentences, and the teach-someone-younger quest where they host the Sprout's first showcase.
materials: a parent with twenty minutes, or Rebut if they want the machine across the table
this week's Sprout family-audience card, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: The formal one
steps.body:
The season's last debate is the formal one: three full rounds, recorded start to finish, no pausing to think off camera. Your opponent is a parent, or Rebut if you want the machine across the table one last time.

Pick your motion before you start, and this season there are two. 'A handmade gift is better than a bought one', argued hours after a handmade gift landed in someone's hands. Or 'One day machines will outthink the people who build them', argued by someone who just spent a season giving a machine its mind. This quest is set up for the first; if you want the second, ask a grown-up to switch it before you begin.

The formal rules, held strictly. Round 1: steelman before you speak, the other side's best argument said so fairly your opponent nods, then your claim, one reason, one example. Round 2: one cross-examination question each, aimed at a real gap. Round 3: one closing point, said once, not three points stacked. Voice rules to the end: speak to the back wall, one pause on purpose, look at your opponent when you answer their point.

When the debate ends, keep the camera up for the book and the season. The book, five minutes: name the title, one thing it changed about how you think, one moment described so a stranger could picture it, and whether a friend should read it. The season, three sentences: one per sprint, the moment from each worth keeping forever.

steps.title: Teach someone younger: run the show
steps.body:
Every showcase this season you ran a parent card with a younger sibling, cousin or friend, or a parent playing the part. Today is bigger: they have their own first showcase, and you are not the helper. You are the host.

Read the family-audience card all the way through first, so you know the show's three acts: the count to 10, their best pattern clapped, and their favorite sound. Set the room like it matters: family sitting as a real audience, them standing where everyone can see.

Then host it. Introduce the star, run the acts in order, and lead the applause after each one. One rule beats all the others: it is their show. They count, they clap, they pick the sound, at their speed, in their way, and a wobble in the middle of the count is part of the act, not a problem to fix. If they go shy, do the act with them once, then hand it back.

Close the show the card's way: read Hello Ruby aloud to them in front of everyone, and make sure the star lands the way it always does. The star is for showing.

Watch for one thing they do that surprises you. You have watched them all season from the corner of your eye; tonight you get the front row.
checklist: I read the card all the way through before the show
The family sat as a real audience and they stood where all could see
They did every act themselves, at their own speed, and I led the applause
I read Hello Ruby aloud to close, and the star was for showing
I noticed one thing they did that surprised me

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the full formal debate, all three rounds, then the five minutes on the book, then your three season sentences, one per sprint. Phone propped up, whole face in frame, no cuts.
